source_read: PMC full text PMC6055296 (Public Health Rep 2018;133(4):423–431) in my own browser tab (title checked): abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results, Tables 1 and 2 (rendered as text; Table 2 sums, rank changes and percentage changes recomputed by script on my tab), Discussion, Strengths and Weaknesses, Conclusions, footnotes (conflicts, funding), affiliations and all 20 references. Figures 1–3 are images that had not loaded (not viewed); only values stated in the text were used. Card check only (task has no claims; step 1 empty).

design.note: National death-registration analysis (NVSS multiple-cause micro-data, 1999–2015) with a proportional reallocation model; no linkage or validation.

instrument.note: JBI prevalence fits a census count of certificates. METHODS 5.3 lists 'registry descriptions' under no instrument; the card cites the round's first-reader brief for JBI on certificate studies, which I have not read, so the editor should confirm that this is the round's rule.

key_findings.note: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1 footnote f. Row sums recomputed: opioid 95,467 + 59,410 + 44,868 + 55,782 = 255,527; non-opioid 61,417 + 24,191 = 85,608; with 97,159 and 313 the total is 438,607; 58.3%, 19.5%, 22.2%.
Results, 1st paragraph. Recomputed +400.7%, +149.8%, +220.5%. Editors' calculation checked: 2,255/11,128 = 20.3% (1999), 7,227/44,115 = 16.4% (2015).
Recomputed from Table 1: 59,410 + 55,782 = 115,192 (45.1%); 44,868 + 55,782 = 100,650 (39.4%). Methods, 2nd paragraph says opioid-related deaths could include non-opioid drugs.
Results, 2nd paragraph (all for 2015). The abstract gives the same five states without saying the figure is for 2015.

Results, 3rd paragraph. The paper gives the changes as '%' (0.2% in Louisiana to 42.2% in North Dakota; 0.2% to 12.8%) without saying whether they are percentage points or relative changes; the card's 'points' is an interpretation.

Results, 4th paragraph; Methods, 4th paragraph. 'More than doubled' in the five states must refer to the 1999–2015 totals (Figure 3, not viewable): in 2015 Table 2 gives +94% for Alabama and +55% for Mississippi. Pennsylvania: 20,521 − 11,152 = 9,369 reported, so +119%.

Table 2 summed on my tab: reported 29,383 (equal to the national 2015 opioid count), reallocated 5,662. The five 'less than 1%' states recompute to 0.6%–0.9% (printed as 0 or 1); the five 'over 50%' states recompute to 94, 85, 55, 99 and 103%.
Results, 6th paragraph; Table 2: 8 zeros, 15 positive values printed, Idaho printed −2 for 45th to 43rd; ranks 1–51 are each used once in both columns.

reporting_issues.note: The all-deaths wording also appears in Abstract › Methods and in Strengths and Weaknesses, 1st paragraph. A national check gives the same result as the card's Pennsylvania check: 255,527/341,135 = 0.749, × 97,159 ≈ 72,800 ('more than 70,000'); with all deaths as denominator, 0.583 × 97,159 ≈ 56,600.
Recounted on my tab: 15 printed positives, 28 negatives, 8 zeros; with Idaho's sign corrected, 16 up and 27 down, and the changes then sum to zero.
Recomputed: in 2015 California + Florida + Ohio + Pennsylvania + Texas = 2,674 of 5,662 (47.2%); the top five in 2015 are Pennsylvania 1,307, Florida 538, California 450, Indiana 404, New Jersey 365.
Ref 9 is Ruhm 2016 (Popul Health Metrics, 1999–2012); the 2014 state analysis is presumably Ruhm 2017 (Am J Prev Med), which is not in the reference list.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high, for the reallocated estimate, as the card reasons. Low risk only for what the certificates say. Item judgments checked; item 8's 'internally consistent' rates confirmed (no percentage change differs from the recomputation by more than 1 point).

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. The Conclusions' 'have been missed' is firmer than the body's 'could be categorized'; the card records this.

missed: The rates in Table 2 are not described as crude or age-adjusted, and no population source is named. The populations implied by the table (for example 261 deaths at 5.37 per 100,000 gives 4.86 million for Alabama) fit 2015 state populations, so the rates appear crude and should not be set beside CDC's age-adjusted rates.

Discussion, 4th paragraph: Kentucky's opioid codes rising 43% and unspecified reporting falling 28% over 1999–2015 (points or relative change not stated) are read as showing that 'state-based efforts can improve' drug-specific reporting. This is a before-and-after trend in one state with no comparison.

Correction (funding.affiliations_note): two authors are at the University of Pittsburgh Graduate School of Public Health, but only Buchanich is listed in the Department of Biostatistics (Burke's affiliation is the school). For Williams the article gives only the Office of the Medical Examiner of Allegheny County; that he certifies deaths is not stated in the article.

Context for the replication timeline: Buchanich is a co-author of the Slavova et al. 2019 review that relays this paper's 70,000 estimate (card sc_slavova_2019), so that review is not independent support.
